title: The map that missed the pump
note: Fictional unit and patients. DRAFT pending clinical sign-off. Your unit protocol, the attending nephrologist and your local disaster authorities decide every real event.
intro: You are the safety nurse of a 20-station unit in San Fernando, Pampanga, running the annual hazard and dependency review before typhoon season with the water treatment and biomedical technicians. The generator log shows a monthly test, each one “passed.”

n1.prompt: How do you check the power line on the dependency map?

choices.text: Walk the electrical panel with both technicians and run the generator under real load, with the water system running, while watching the loop pressure.
choices.feedback: Testing the whole chain is the only way to see what the generator really carries. A voltage check on an unloaded generator misses dependencies.

choices.text: Accept the monthly log: it says “passed” every month.
choices.feedback: The log tests the generator alone, not what it feeds. That is how this unit missed the problem.
choices.then: The head nurse asks you to run a loaded test anyway.

choices.text: Ask the technicians whether everything important is on the generator circuit.
choices.feedback: Asking helps, but people often assume. Walk the panel and test under load to be sure.
choices.then: The technicians are not sure about the booster pump, so you run a loaded test.

n2.scene: Eleven minutes into the loaded test, every machine in rinse mode alarms for low water pressure. The booster pump that feeds the reverse osmosis system is on the utility breaker, not the generator circuit.
n2.prompt: What do you do with this finding?

choices.text: Report it to the unit manager and the Dialysis Clinical Head today, with an interim plan (fill the storage tank before storms, a manual transfer step in the outage protocol) and a date to rewire the pump onto the generator circuit.
choices.feedback: A single point of failure that could stop every treatment is reported the day it is found, with an interim plan and an owner.

choices.text: Note it for next year’s budget meeting.
choices.feedback: Typhoon season is weeks away. A known gap that stops all treatment cannot wait a year.
choices.then: The unit manager hears about it and asks for an interim plan this week.

choices.text: Leave it: in a real outage the storage tank usually lasts long enough.
choices.feedback: The tank lasted eleven minutes. Patients would be connected when the water stops, which turns an outage into an emergency take-off.
choices.then: The Dialysis Clinical Head overrules you and orders an interim plan and rewiring.

n3.scene: The rewiring is scheduled for next month.
n3.prompt: How do you update the dependency map and the test?

choices.text: Draw the power–water “fail together” line on the map, mark the pump as a single point of failure until rewired, and change the monthly test to run under load with the water system and loop pressure checked.
choices.feedback: The map should show what fails together, and the test should test the whole chain so the gap cannot hide again.
The map is right, but an unchanged test would miss the next gap.
choices.then: You add the loaded test to the protocol as well.

choices.text: Leave the map unchanged until the rewiring is done.
choices.feedback: Until the fix, the map must show the risk; staff plan from it.
choices.then: You update it after the head nurse asks.

end.title: Before the season
end.text: The pump is moved onto the generator circuit before typhoon season, the map shows the line, and the monthly test now runs under load. The next brownout passes without a single alarm.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Test the whole chain, not one machine: a generator test with no load misses what it feeds.
  • Report a single point of failure the day you find it, with an interim plan, an owner and a date.
  • Draw what fails together on the map, so the next person sees it.
